routes.description: Establish that Christianity can coherently recognize suffering as genuinely wrong within a broken creation while relating it to human freedom, divine presence, justice, and promised restoration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the framework explains why suffering is real evil without requiring a purpose for every tragedy, preserves divine goodness and power, and connects present brokenness to morally adequate divine action and future healing.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Christian account makes coherent overall sense of suffering alongside an all-powerful and all-loving God.

centralBridges.description: Explain how a good creation can be presently broken and why its natural mechanisms can produce suffering without making suffering morally illusory.
Account for divine love through God's presence with sufferers, participation in suffering, and action against evil rather than through a distinct benefit assigned to every tragedy.
Show how resurrection, judgment, forgiveness, and future restoration can heal suffering and put wrongs right without disregarding victims or consequences.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground the judgment that suffering and exploitation are objectively wrong rather than merely evolutionarily disfavored.
Explain the roles of consequential human freedom and incomplete present healing within the wider broken-world framework.

routes.description: Establish that suffering is expected under naturalism but creates unresolved tensions among divine omnipotence, perfect love, selective intervention, judgment, and the claimed final defeat of evil.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if apparently gratuitous suffering and the Christian framework's treatment of healing and salvation remain less compatible with an all-powerful, all-loving God than with naturalistic expectations.

motionBridge.description: Show that the observed reality and distribution of suffering make belief in the specified Christian God unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish why an omnipotent and perfectly loving God would need a morally sufficient account of every evil that God knowingly permits.
Show that natural processes can explain suffering and human aversion to it without invoking divine purposes or transcendent moral explanation.
Test whether selective and ambiguous recoveries provide evidence of divine intervention rather than outcomes expected from natural uncertainty.
Determine whether judgment based on belief or reconciliation treats sincere unbelief and grave wrongdoing consistently with perfect love and proportionate justice.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Examine whether changing Christian moral practice weakens the claimed explanatory advantage of an objective divine standard.
Assess whether promised resurrection and future healing are sufficiently warranted to resolve rather than postpone the evidential problem.

sections.title: Suffering, naturalism, and the coherence of a broken creation
sections.rationale: This section contains the motion's foundational clash over whether naturalism adequately accommodates suffering or whether Christian broken-creation claims better explain both its mechanisms and its status as a genuine wrong.

sections.title: Evolution, objective morality, and human dignity
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of moral aversion, cooperation, objective norms, and equal dignity bear on whether Christianity supplies explanatory resources that naturalism lacks and whether its historical record affects that claim.

sections.title: Divine presence, permitted evil, and future restoration
sections.rationale: The issue tests whether divine solidarity, epistemic limits, resurrection, and eventual healing can reconcile perfect goodness with permitted atrocities, or whether every permitted evil still demands an adequate greater-good justification.

sections.title: Unanswered prayer and evidence of divine healing
sections.rationale: Selective recovery provides a concrete test of the broken-world and partially realized kingdom account against the contention that natural uncertainty predicts the observed pattern better than purposeful divine intervention.

sections.title: Judgment, forgiveness, freedom, and sincere unbelief
sections.rationale: This section examines whether divine judgment, costly forgiveness, human freedom, and an inclusive invitation can secure justice for victims while treating sincere unbelievers and repentant wrongdoers consistently with perfect love.
